title: Bella's schooling in Biloxi and strict lessons
summary: She went to ninth grade, was pushed by her father, used McGuffey books, and laments people who cannot read.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: And he just looked at me. He said, where you come from? I said, Bluxy. He said, you went to school? I said, I went to ninth grade and I walked a whole mile with Brogan shoes on, bravest tips. And he just looked at me. He said, well, you... He said, your education is pretty good. I went to ninth grade and I wanted to go to college. When my mother died and left my dad was 16th year old, that made me and my biggest sister had to work. But don't you think we don't know how to read and write and figure? I know if I... And I know some girls right now, white girls, where I used to work at, they'd go to college and they'd come in my bedroom at night and I said, Bella, I said, what? Show me how to do this. I said, well, y'all going to college? And they don't know good as me and you know. That's true, ain't it? Yeah. They don't know good as you. Because, see, when we went to school, we had the lawn. Now when they go to school, they exercise us and all that. We didn't do that. We went to school. We stayed in there. Twelve o'clock we come out and we eat us lunch. We go back in for one o'clock. And three o'clock, my papa be right there with the wagon and the horse to get us. You hear me? And don't you think we sat up in that kitchen that night in that dining room and he sat there with a trap. And he made us study that lesson. He said, y'all didn't grow up here. And I see some girls come up with, when I come up, they don't know how to hear from a V. Right there. Get into college, they can hardly read. Miss Neal would tell me get letters, they come in. Boom, boom, boom, boom. Miss Bella read my letter. Ain't that's pitiful? Oh, I think that's pitiful. For people that have to, you know, read.
Well, some people didn't get the chance though. Some people didn't have the chance to go to school.

Well, I didn't want to go to school. My papa beat me and made me go. Now I'm glad today I went. I didn't want to go. Oh, that lesson was hard. We had the McGuffey's books and the McGuffey's spellers. They don't have that no more. I've seen them though. My mother saved her. Oh, oh, oh. I had two I saved. They over the lake against my sister and them guys. Oh, them things was hard to spell. And they put, put about that much on the blank book. Put numbers. From there, way down to there and then they draw that line.

Now you had that to count up and you better have it straight. If you didn't, they stand you to the board and make you write your name like my name was Isabella. They make me write a hundred times and I look at the teacher. She said, now you write on that side. I said, I said, how many? She said, write clean till your daddy come. And then when my daddy come again, we go home, my papa whoop him. Cause I had right to know it. See?
